title: Directions and Distance Reasoning — Part 7 of 10

questions.question: What does '3D direction reasoning' add beyond standard compass-based problems?
options: A third dimension (such as elevation or altitude), in addition to the usual horizontal direction
Nothing new
It removes the need for distance
It only applies to underground problems
questions.rationale: 3D direction reasoning introduces a vertical dimension (elevation/altitude) on top of the standard horizontal compass directions.

questions.question: What is a 'coordinate transformation'?
options: Deleting a point's coordinates
A synonym for distance
Converting a position from one coordinate system or reference frame into another
Only used for time conversions
questions.rationale: A coordinate transformation converts a position's representation from one coordinate system or reference frame into an equivalent one in a different system.

questions.question: What is a 'spatial proof trace'?
options: A physical trail marker
A step-by-step record of how a spatial conclusion (like a direction or distance) was derived
A synonym for a spatial graph
A type of map projection
questions.rationale: A spatial proof trace records the sequence of steps taken to derive a spatial conclusion, supporting both verification and explanation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'verification' step in spatial reasoning?
options: To make the process take longer
To generate a random alternative answer
To convert units automatically
Confirming the derived answer is consistent with all the original spatial constraints
questions.rationale: Verification checks the derived answer against every original spatial constraint to confirm it is genuinely consistent, not just superficially plausible.

questions.question: What does the 'triangle inequality check' verify about a set of distances?
options: That no one distance between two points exceeds the sum of the distances via a third point, which would be geometrically impossible
That all distances are equal
That every distance is a whole number
That directions are all cardinal (N/S/E/W)
questions.rationale: The triangle inequality states that the direct distance between two points can never exceed the sum of the distances through a third point — a violation signals an impossible or inconsistent set of distances.

questions.question: Why is the triangle inequality a useful validation tool in distance reasoning?
options: It has no practical use
It only applies to time problems
It can immediately flag an impossible or inconsistent set of stated distances
It replaces the need for coordinates entirely
questions.rationale: Checking the triangle inequality gives a quick, purely mathematical way to catch a set of stated distances that couldn't possibly all be true together.

questions.question: What is demonstrated by a 'complete example' combining several prior direction-and-distance concepts?
options: Nothing beyond what's already been said
How the parsing, representation, and constraint-solving steps combine to solve a realistic multi-step problem
Only how to draw a compass rose
That verification is unnecessary for real problems
questions.rationale: A complete example shows how the individually-introduced concepts — parsing, representation-building, constraint solving — combine in practice to solve a realistic, non-trivial problem.

questions.question: In an 'example with turns,' why must both the sequence and the magnitude of each turn be tracked accurately?
options: Neither actually matters for the final answer
Because turns don't affect distance calculations
Because only the first turn matters
Because an error in either the order or the degree of a turn changes the final heading and therefore the final position
questions.rationale: Both the order in which turns occur and their exact degree matter — getting either wrong changes the final heading, and therefore the final computed position.

questions.question: Why might a spatial reasoning problem require converting between coordinate systems mid-solution?
options: This never happens in practice
Because different parts of the problem may naturally be described in different reference frames (e.g., local vs global)
Because coordinate systems are purely cosmetic
Because conversions are only needed at the very start
questions.rationale: Different parts of a problem might naturally be expressed in different reference frames, requiring a conversion partway through to combine them consistently.

questions.question: What is the benefit of an explicit proof trace when solving a complex, multi-step spatial problem?
options: There is no real benefit
It allows each individual step to be checked, making it easier to locate exactly where an error occurred
It automatically corrects any mistakes
It removes the need for the triangle inequality check
questions.rationale: An explicit trace exposes every intermediate step, making it much easier to pinpoint exactly where an error was introduced if the final answer turns out to be wrong.
